_readme: Topics for the Daily Topic view. Each topic is [title, what it is, question to think about]. Add your own topics or niches freely.

niches.label: Tech and AI
topics: Hallucination in language models
Why an AI model can state something false with full confidence.
Explain why it happens and how a user can protect themselves from it.
Open weights versus closed models
Some AI models can be downloaded and run by anyone; others sit behind an API.
Which approach is better for society, and who gains from each?
The cost of a single AI answer
Every reply from a large model uses real electricity, chips and water.
Should heavy AI use be priced by what it actually consumes?
Retrieval-augmented generation
Giving a model documents to read before it answers, instead of relying on memory.
Explain it to a friend using a library and a student as the picture.
Deepfakes and trust
Synthetic video and voice are now cheap enough for anyone to make.
How should an ordinary person decide what to believe online?
Edge computing
Running the computation on the device itself rather than in a far-away data centre.
When does it matter that your phone does the thinking, not the cloud?
Vendor lock-in
The cost of leaving a platform once your data and habits live inside it.
Describe a lock-in you are in right now and what leaving would cost.
Technical debt
Shortcuts in code that save time today and charge interest later.
When is taking on technical debt the right decision?
End-to-end encryption
Only the sender and receiver can read the message; even the service cannot.
Should governments be able to demand a way in?
AI agents that act for you
Software that does not just answer but books, buys and sends on your behalf.
What would you let an agent do without asking you first, and what never?
The attention economy
Apps earn money from the minutes you spend, so they are designed to hold you.
Is it the user's job or the designer's job to fix this?
Benchmarks and what they hide
A test score tells you how a model did on that test, not how it will do for you.
Why can a model top a leaderboard and still disappoint in real work?

niches.label: Computer science
topics: Why binary
Computers use two states because two are easy to tell apart reliably.
Explain to a 12-year-old why computers count in zeros and ones.
Caching
Keeping a copy of an answer nearby so you do not have to fetch it again.
Give three everyday examples of caching that are not about computers.
The halting problem
No program can decide, for every possible program, whether it will ever finish.
Why is it useful to know that some problems cannot be solved at all?
Hash functions
Turning any input into a short fixed-size fingerprint.
Explain how a website can check your password without storing it.
Race conditions
A bug that appears only when two things happen in an unlucky order.
Describe one with a real-life picture, such as two people booking the last seat.
Compilers versus interpreters
Translate the whole program first, or translate and run it line by line.
Which would you choose for a beginner language, and why?
Big-O in daily life
A way to say how the work grows as the pile gets bigger.
Compare two ways of finding a name in a phone book using Big-O.
Abstraction
Hiding detail so you can think about one layer at a time.
Explain driving a car as a stack of abstractions.
Idempotence
Doing something twice has the same effect as doing it once.
Why should a payment button be idempotent?
The CAP theorem
A distributed database cannot promise consistency, availability and partition tolerance all at once.
Which would you give up for a banking app, and which for a social feed?
Recursion
Solving a problem by solving a smaller copy of the same problem.
Teach recursion using Russian dolls or a queue of people.
Garbage collection
The runtime automatically frees memory that the program can no longer reach.
What do you gain and what do you lose compared with managing memory yourself?

niches.label: Psychology
topics: Confirmation bias
We notice evidence that agrees with us and wave away the rest.
Describe a belief you held too long and what finally changed it.
The spotlight effect
We overestimate how much other people notice us.
How would your behaviour change if you truly believed nobody was watching?
Sunk cost
Continuing something because of what you already spent, not what you will gain.
When is finishing what you started wisdom, and when is it a trap?
Hedonic adaptation
We get used to good and bad changes faster than we expect.
What does this mean for how you should spend money?
The planning fallacy
We predict tasks will take less time than they always do.
How do you plan a project knowing your estimate is wrong?
Learned helplessness
After repeated failure, people stop trying even when escape is possible.
How do you help someone, or yourself, unlearn it?
Social proof
We decide what is correct by looking at what others are doing.
Where does following the crowd help you, and where does it hurt?
The Dunning-Kruger effect
Beginners often overrate themselves because they cannot yet see what they are missing.
How can you tell whether you are good at something or just early?
Loss aversion
Losing a hundred hurts more than gaining a hundred pleases.
Give an example where fear of loss made you choose badly.
Cognitive dissonance
The discomfort of holding two beliefs, or a belief and an action, that clash.
Describe a time you changed a belief to match what you had already done.
Intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation
Doing something for its own sake versus for a reward.
Can paying someone for a hobby ruin it?
The bystander effect
The more people present, the less likely any one of them helps.
What would you say out loud to break it in an emergency?

niches.label: Money and economics
topics: Inflation
The same note buys a little less every year.
Explain why keeping all your savings in cash is not actually safe.
Index funds
Buying a small slice of the whole market instead of picking winners.
Why do most professionals fail to beat this simple approach?
Incentives
People respond to what is rewarded, not to what is intended.
Describe a rule that backfired because of the incentive it created.
Supply and demand
Price is where what sellers will accept meets what buyers will pay.
Use it to explain why concert tickets are resold at high prices.
The rule of 72
Divide 72 by the interest rate to get the years needed to double money.
Show how this changes the way you see a loan or an investment.
Good debt and bad debt
Borrowing to buy something that grows versus something that shrinks.
Is an education loan good debt? Argue both sides.
Comparative advantage
Everyone gains when each does what they give up the least to do.
Why should a great programmer still hire someone to do their accounts?
Externalities
A cost or benefit that lands on someone who was not part of the deal.
Who should pay for the pollution from a factory you buy from?
Buy now, pay later
Splitting a purchase into small instalments with little friction.
Is it a helpful tool or a trap for young earners?
Scarcity
There is never enough time, money or attention for everything.
What are you scarce in right now, and what are you trading it for?
Universal basic income
Every adult receives a regular payment with no conditions attached.
Would people stop working? Make the case for and against.
Insurance
Paying a small certain amount to avoid a large uncertain loss.
Which insurance is worth it at 22 and which is not?

niches.label: Startups and business
topics: Solving your own problem
Many products begin as a fix for something the founder was annoyed by.
What annoys you weekly that someone would pay to have fixed?
Distribution beats product
A decent product people hear about usually beats a great one nobody finds.
How would you get the first hundred users for a new app with no budget?
Pricing
The price is a message about who the product is for.
When is charging more the kinder thing to do for your customer?
Moats
What stops a competitor from copying you and taking your customers.
Pick a company you use and name its moat.
Pivoting
Changing direction while keeping what you learned.
How do you tell a needed pivot from giving up too early?
Bootstrapping versus funding
Growing on your own revenue or taking investor money to grow faster.
Which would you choose for your first company, and what would you trade away?
Talking to users
Asking people about their real past behaviour instead of their opinions.
What is a question that gets honest answers about a product idea?
Churn
The share of customers who leave in a given period.
Why can a business with fast sign-ups still be dying?
The freemium model
The basic product is free and a small share of users pay for more.
Where should the line between free and paid be drawn?
First-mover advantage
Being first gives a head start but also the cost of teaching the market.
Name a market where the first company lost and explain why.
Freelancing as a business
Selling your skill directly, one client at a time.
How does a student find their first paying client?
Marketplaces and the cold start
A marketplace is useless to buyers without sellers and to sellers without buyers.
How would you start one from zero?

niches.label: Science
topics: The scientific method
Guess, predict, test, and be willing to be wrong.
Describe how you would test a claim you saw on social media.
Entropy
Left alone, things move from order to disorder.
Explain why your room gets messy by itself but never tidy by itself.
Natural selection
Traits that help survival and reproduction become more common over generations.
Explain it without using the phrase survival of the fittest.
Placebo effect
A treatment with no active ingredient can still make people feel better.
Why do medical trials need a placebo group?
Correlation and causation
Two things moving together does not mean one causes the other.
Give an example where confusing the two leads to a bad decision.
The speed of light
Nothing with mass can reach it, and information cannot travel faster.
What does it mean that we see the stars as they were, not as they are?
Vaccines
Training the immune system with a harmless preview of a threat.
Explain herd immunity to someone who is unsure about vaccines.
Plate tectonics
The ground is made of slow-moving plates that collide and pull apart.
Why does northern India have earthquakes and the Himalayas?
The microbiome
Trillions of bacteria live in your gut and affect digestion and more.
What does it change about how you think of your own body?
Climate versus weather
Weather is today's mood; climate is the long-term personality.
Why does one cold winter not disprove global warming?
Half-life
The time it takes for half of a substance to decay.
How do scientists know the age of a fossil?
Black holes
A region where gravity is so strong that not even light escapes.
Explain what an event horizon is using a river and a waterfall.

niches.label: History
topics: The printing press
Cheap copies of text broke the monopoly on knowledge.
Compare its effect to the internet's. What is the same and what is different?
The Indus Valley civilisation
Planned cities with drainage, thousands of years ago, and a script still unread.
What does its town planning tell you about the people?
The Industrial Revolution
Machines and factories replaced hand work and moved people into cities.
Who won and who lost, and what does that say about AI today?
The Silk Road
Trade routes that moved goods, religions, diseases and ideas across continents.
What travelled along it that mattered more than silk?
The partition of India
The 1947 division that displaced millions.
How should a country remember an event that is still painful?
The Cold War space race
Two rivals competing to reach orbit and the Moon.
Did competition achieve what cooperation could not?
The Green Revolution in India
New seeds, fertiliser and irrigation that ended recurring food shortages.
What were the benefits, and what were the hidden costs?
The fall of the Berlin Wall
In 1989 a physical border between two systems came down in one night.
Why do some walls fall suddenly after standing for decades?
Ashoka after Kalinga
An emperor who turned from conquest to public welfare after a bloody war.
Can a leader truly change? What does his story suggest?
The history of zero
A symbol for nothing that made modern mathematics possible.
Why was treating nothing as a number such a big step?
The 1991 economic reforms
India opened its economy after a balance-of-payments crisis.
How did those decisions shape the jobs available to you today?
How the internet began
A research network built to share computers grew into a global utility.
What early design choices still shape the web today?

niches.label: Philosophy and ethics
topics: The trolley problem
Would you divert a runaway trolley to kill one person instead of five?
What does your answer reveal about how you judge right and wrong?
The ship of Theseus
If every plank of a ship is replaced, is it still the same ship?
Are you the same person you were ten years ago?
Stoicism
Focus on what you control and accept what you cannot.
Apply it to an exam result or a job rejection.
Free will
Whether your choices are truly yours or the result of causes you did not choose.
Does it matter for how we punish or reward people?
The veil of ignorance
Design a society without knowing which person in it you will be.
What rules would you choose from behind that veil?
Means and ends
Whether a good result can justify a bad action.
Is it ever right to lie to protect someone?
Karma yoga
Act with full effort and let go of attachment to the result.
Is it possible to care deeply about your work and not about the outcome?
The experience machine
A machine that gives you any experience you want, but none of it is real.
Would you plug in for life? Why or why not?
Privacy as a right
The claim that some parts of life are nobody else's business.
If you have nothing to hide, do you still need privacy?
Moral luck
We judge people for outcomes that were partly out of their hands.
Should a careless driver who hurts no one be judged the same as one who does?
What makes a good life
Pleasure, meaning, virtue and relationships are the usual candidates.
Which would you rank first, and what would you give up for it?
Obligations to future generations
People not yet born will live with the choices made now.
How much should you sacrifice today for someone in 2126?

niches.label: Learning and productivity
topics: Spaced repetition
Reviewing something just as you are about to forget it makes it stick.
How would you use it for your next exam?
Active recall
Testing yourself beats re-reading.
Why does re-reading feel productive while teaching you little?
Deep work
Long stretches of focus on one hard thing with no distractions.
What would have to change in your day to get two hours of it?
The Feynman technique
If you cannot explain it simply, you do not understand it yet.
Pick something you studied this week and explain it to a ten-year-old.
Habit stacking
Attach a new habit to one you already do without thinking.
Design a stack for a habit you keep failing to start.
Procrastination
Putting off a task is usually about avoiding a feeling, not about laziness.
What feeling are you avoiding in the task you keep delaying?
The 80/20 rule
A small part of the effort usually produces most of the result.
What is the 20 percent in your current project?
Tutorial hell
Watching one course after another without building anything.
How do you know when to stop learning and start making?
Deliberate practice
Practising the exact thing you are bad at, with feedback.
How is it different from simply putting in hours?
Sleep and memory
The brain files the day's learning while you sleep.
Is an all-night study session ever worth it?
Saying no
Every yes spends time you could have used elsewhere.
What should you stop doing this month?
Learning in public
Sharing what you learn as you learn it.
What are the risks and rewards of posting unfinished work?

niches.label: Health and fitness
topics: Progressive overload
Muscles grow when the demand on them rises a little over time.
How do you apply it with only bodyweight at home?
Protein on a vegetarian diet
Dal, paneer, soy, curd and legumes can cover protein needs with planning.
Plan a day of eating that reaches your protein target without meat.
Calories in, calories out
Weight change follows the gap between energy eaten and energy used.
Why is it true and still not the whole story?
Sleep debt
Lost sleep builds up and affects mood, memory and appetite.
What would you change tonight to sleep an hour more?
Consistency over intensity
A modest plan you follow beats a perfect plan you quit.
What is the smallest workout you could never skip?
Posture and the desk
Long sitting shortens some muscles and weakens others.
What three movements would you give a student who sits all day?
Hydration myths
The eight-glasses rule is a rough guide, not a law.
How do you actually know if you are drinking enough?
Stress and the body
Short stress sharpens you; constant stress wears you down.
How does exam stress show up in your body, and what helps?
Walking
The most underrated exercise: low risk, easy to repeat, good for the mind.
Make the case for a daily walk to someone who only lifts.
Sugar
Added sugar is easy to overeat because it does not make you feel full.
Where is the hidden sugar in a normal Indian day of eating?
Rest days
Muscle is built during recovery, not during the workout.
Why is resting part of training rather than a break from it?
Screens and the eyes
Close focus for hours tires the eyes and dries them out.
What habits would protect a programmer's eyes for forty years?

niches.label: India and society
topics: UPI
Instant bank-to-bank payments from a phone, at almost no cost.
Why did it succeed in India when similar systems struggled elsewhere?
Brain drain
Skilled people leaving for better pay and facilities abroad.
Is it a loss for India or a long-term gain?
Coaching culture
Years of paid coaching aimed at a single entrance exam.
What does it teach well, and what does it cost students?
English as a gatekeeper
Fluency in English opens doors that skill alone often cannot.
Is that fair, and what should a student do about it?
The gig economy
Delivery and ride work paid per task, with freedom and little security.
Are gig workers independent, or employees without benefits?
Aadhaar and digital identity
A single number linking a person to many services.
Where is the line between convenience and surveillance?
Urban migration
Millions move from villages to cities for work every year.
What does a city owe the people who build and run it?
Air pollution
Many Indian cities spend winters with hazardous air.
Who should act first: the citizen, the city or the nation?
Linguistic diversity
Hundreds of languages and no single one spoken by everyone.
Is this a strength, a problem, or both?
Reservation
Seats set aside in education and jobs for historically excluded groups.
State the strongest argument for it and the strongest against it.
Social media and elections
Campaigns now reach voters directly, one feed at a time.
Does this make democracy stronger or easier to manipulate?
The demographic dividend
A young population can power growth, if there are jobs and skills.
What must happen in the next ten years for it to pay off?

niches.label: Career and communication
topics: Tell me about yourself
The first interview question, and the one most people answer worst.
Give your answer in ninety seconds: present, past, future.
Your biggest weakness
A real weakness, what it cost you, and what you are doing about it.
Answer honestly without turning it into a hidden boast.
Explaining a project
Problem, what you built, the hard part, and the result.
Explain one of your projects to someone who does not code.
Disagreeing with a senior
Raising a concern respectfully and still being heard.
How would you tell your team lead that their plan has a flaw?
Asking for help
A good question shows what you tried and exactly where you are stuck.
Turn 'it is not working' into a question worth answering.
Negotiating a salary
Knowing your number, their range, and what else is on the table.
How does a fresher negotiate without experience to point to?
Networking without being fake
Building relationships by being useful and curious.
How would you message a stranger whose career you admire?
Handling a failure story
What happened, what you owned, and what changed afterwards.
Tell the story of a failure in a way that makes someone trust you more.
Giving feedback
Specific, about the work, and delivered soon.
How do you tell a friend their code or essay is not good?
Why this company
Showing you understand what they do and where you fit.
Pick a company you like and answer in one minute.
Generalist or specialist
Knowing a little about much, or much about a little.
Which should a first-year MCA student aim for?
Remote work
Freedom and focus on one side, isolation and blurred hours on the other.
Would you take a remote first job? Argue both sides.
